articles.title: US announces nationwide rail infrastructure investment
articles.summary: The US Department of Transportation has announced a US$2.3 billion investment covering freight and passenger rail projects across 45 states and the District of Columbia. The funding will be distributed through the Federal Railroad Administration’s Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements Grant...
articles.body: The US Department of Transportation has announced a US$2.3 billion investment covering freight and passenger rail projects across 45 states and the District of Columbia. The funding will be distributed through the Federal Railroad Administration’s Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements Grant Programme. The latest funding round includes 105 projects and is expected to support improvements across more than 2,000 miles of railway track. State, local and private partners will provide an additional US$1.9 billion in non-federal funding. Freight rail and port projects Several projects focus on freight corridors, short-line railways and port connections. Recipient Funding Project Arkansas & Missouri Railroad Company US$33.6 million Track rehabilitation between Fort Smith, Arkansas, and Monett, Missouri Wheeling & Lake Erie Railway US$43.5 million Rehabilitation and modernisation of the Toledo Swing Bridge in Ohio Maine Department of Transportation US$37 million Rehabilitation of approximately 90 miles of railway in northern Maine Aberdeen Carolina & Western Railway US$20 million Track, bridge and crossing upgrades in North Carolina Texas City Terminal Railway Company US$30 million Entrance-gate realignment and rail yard rehabilitation and expansion Wisconsin Department of Transportation US$218 million Track, bridge, crossing and station improvements under the Hiawatha West project The Arkansas and Missouri project will replace rail and sleepers, improve siding infrastructure and install rail lubricators on high-degree curves. In Ohio, the Toledo Swing Bridge project will rehabilitate eight of the bridge’s 11 spans and replace its timber fender systems. The work will enable the bridge to accommodate railcars weighing up to 286,000 pounds. Maine will use its funding to replace rail, sleepers and ballast along approximately 90 miles of track. The project also includes the rehabilitation of a railway bridge deck. The North Carolina project will install approximately 30 miles of continuous welded rail, rehabilitate bridges and modernise level-crossing signals. Port-related freight improvements Texas City Terminal Railway Company will realign the vehicle entrance gate serving the port area and rehabilitate and expand its railway yard. The project aims to address safety conflicts between trains and vehicles entering a petroleum facility. It will also provide additional capacity for petrochemical exports. US Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy said the investment would improve short-line railway infrastructure, port connections and rail safety across the country. Federal Railroad Administration Administrator David Fink added that the funding would help short-line railways modernise their daily operations, reduce congestion and improve network performance.

The funding will be distributed through the Federal Railroad Administration’s Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements Grant Programme.
The latest funding round includes 105 projects and is expected to support improvements across more than 2,000 miles of railway track.

articles.title: Eastern Pacific takes wraps off first ammonia dual-fuel VLAC
articles.summary: Idan Ofer’s Eastern Pacific Shipping (EPS) has named its first ammonia dual-fuel very large ammonia carrier (VLAC) at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries in South Korea, bringing the 93,000 cu m vessel closer to its commercial debut. The Singapore-based owner christened the vessel Terra Clove at the Ulsan yard, with delivery...
articles.body: Asia Gas Eastern Pacific takes wraps off first ammonia dual-fuel VLAC Adis Ajdin October 22, 2026 0 0 1 minute read EPS / MMMCZCS EPS / MMMCZCS Idan Ofer’s Eastern Pacific Shipping (EPS) has named its first ammonia dual-fuel very large ammonia carrier (VLAC) at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries in South Korea, bringing the 93,000 cu m vessel closer to its commercial debut. The Singapore-based owner christened the vessel Terra Clove at the Ulsan yard, with delivery scheduled for November following sea trials. The newbuilding is the first ammonia dual-fuel commercial vessel to be registered under the Singapore flag and the first of two such ships being built by HD Hyundai for EPS. Designed to transport ammonia as cargo and burn it as propulsion fuel, the 230 m long vessel is fitted with Everllence’s 6G60ME-LGIA two-stroke engine, which completed factory acceptance testing in April and passed type approval testing in June. The ship features four cargo tanks and dedicated ammonia fuel handling and safety systems, including leak detection and emissions management equipment. The project dates back to June 2022, when EPS joined forces with the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA), HD Hyundai Heavy Industries and classification society ABS to develop an ammonia-powered gas carrier. The partners have since worked on the vessel’s design, safety requirements and regulatory approval, with particular attention to ammonia handling, ventilation, emissions and crew preparedness. The milestone also coincided with EPS signing a strategic partnership with the Mærsk Mc-Kinney Møller Center for Zero Carbon Shipping during the naming ceremony. The two will collaborate on alternative fuels, dual-fuel propulsion, energy efficiency and ammonia safety, including research into methane and ammonia emissions. A joint white paper covering VLAC design, operational safety and crew training is expected later this year. The development adds to EPS’s expanding position in the ammonia carrier market. Earlier this year, the company returned to China’s Jiangnan Shipyard for two additional 90,000 cu m VLACs, scheduled for delivery in the first half of 2028. Those vessels will feature LPG dual-fuel propulsion, rather than engines designed to burn ammonia. The latest contract followed a series of six 93,000 cu m VLACs previously booked at Jiangnan, as EPS continued building up its gas carrier fleet alongside investments in alternative propulsion technologies. articles.title: Shipowners warn fuel transition could slip beyond 2030 as methanol demand remains uncertain
articles.summary: Regulatory uncertainty and limited shipbuilding capacity could delay the wider adoption of alternative marine fuels beyond 2030, shipping executives said, while orders for methanol-capable vessels may not translate directly into demand for the fuel. articles.body: Shipowners warn fuel transition could slip beyond 2030 as methanol demand remains uncertain in International Shipping News 22/10/2026 Regulatory uncertainty and limited shipbuilding capacity could delay the wider adoption of alternative marine fuels beyond 2030, shipping executives said, while orders for methanol-capable vessels may not translate directly into demand for the fuel. Speaking at the tenth Annual International Shipping Forum in Pudong, Shanghai, Safe Bulkers president Loukas Barmparis said ambiguity over decarbonization rules and heavily booked shipyards would delay the transition, pointing to a period after 2030 toward 2035. He described maritime decarbonization as “somehow stalled,” with progress currently concentrated on improving the energy efficiency of existing ships and newer vessel designs. Uncertainty over the International Maritime Organization’s decisions had held back ordering before prompting owners to choose conventional vessels, said Dario Bocchetti, Grimaldi Group’s head of energy-saving, research and design, and ship design. Similarly, Pacific Carriers Limited CEO and managing director Hor Weng Yew said owners could focus on improving fuel efficiency while weighing longer-term fuel decisions. “Making an irreversible commitment when the fuel pathways, infrastructure, and economics are still evolving… I think that’s tough,” Hor said. However, owners could retrofit ships and work with charterers to improve efficiency without waiting for a final fuel pathway, he said. “That’s something shipowners can very well do, very much in their control.” Orders may not translate to demand Meanwhile, dual-fuel vessels, such as new methanol-capable orders, may not ensure that a new ship will operate entirely on methanol, Bocchetti added. Fuel costs and logistics would determine actual use, while producers need demand from more than a handful of owners to support supply growth. “Nevertheless, we have to start it; otherwise, we will never do it,” he said. DNV said more than 294 methanol-capable vessels were on order globally as of August 2026, making methanol the second-largest alternative-fuel technology in the orderbook after LNG, based on its latest Maritime Forecast to 2050, released in August. The figure stood at 991 for LNG-capable vessels, 42 ammonia-capable, and 25 hydrogen-capable vessels. The forecast puts shipping’s low-greenhouse-gas fuel demand, covering low-GHG fuels collectively, at 4 million–22 million mt of oil equivalent in 2030, depending on regulatory outcomes. DNV noted that scaling production depends on confidence that demand will materialize. It also said the existing fleet and orderbook would largely determine which fuels shipping can consume in 2030. Marine Plus president and CEO Dimitris Vranopoulos said fuel supply and trading patterns would continue to constrain owners’ investment in dual-fuel vessels. “Even post-2030, it will be quite difficult and challenging,” Vranopoulos said, adding that “everything has to be synchronized.” Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, assessed Singapore low-carbon methanol at $1,040/mt Oct. 19, unchanged from the prior session, while low-carbon methanol FOB Shanghai was also assessed stable day over day at $815/mt on thin trade. articles.title: Goldman Sachs sees crude freight rates surge to $20 per barrel
articles.summary: Global average crude freight rates have climbed above $20 per barrel from $3 per barrel a year ago, according to Goldman Sachs analysis released Wednesday. The increase initially started in the very large crude carrier segment and on Middle Eastern routes before spreading to all major crude trading routes,...
articles.body: Goldman Sachs sees crude freight rates surge to $20 per barrel in International Shipping News 22/10/2026 Global average crude freight rates have climbed above $20 per barrel from $3 per barrel a year ago, according to Goldman Sachs analysis released Wednesday. The increase initially started in the very large crude carrier segment and on Middle Eastern routes before spreading to all major crude trading routes, particularly affecting long-haul voyages. The bank identified five main drivers behind the $20 per barrel year-over-year surge in the average global crude freight rate. A war risk premium in Hormuz accounts for $7 per barrel, representing one-third of the increase in the global average crude freight rate. Ship-to-ship transfers outside the Persian Gulf that tie up tankers for longer add $4 per barrel, while higher maritime fuel prices contribute another $4 per barrel. Inefficient tanker allocation and increased tanker redirections account for $3 per barrel, and the blockage of the Iranian fleet adds $2 per barrel by boosting demand for non-sanctioned crude tankers. While global freight rates have declined slightly in recent days, likely due to an easing in the risk premium, the global average remains seven times higher than a year ago. Goldman Sachs expects these factors to continue supporting global freight rates as long as the conflict in the Middle East persists. The bank noted that high freight rates may reduce refiners’ overall demand for crude or shift it towards more closely located crude suppliers. Most traded crude benchmarks do not directly include transportation costs in their prices, as they are priced on a free-on-board basis. Goldman Sachs sees high freight rates widening crude price differentials by changing crude trading patterns and supporting refined product prices while suppressing refiners’ net margins. Crude producers with greater dependence on distant buyers may need to discount their crude more heavily to retain demand from refiners facing high transportation costs. Refiners with greater dependence on imported crude from distant suppliers would need to either pass higher freight costs on to final consumers or accept lower net refinery margins. articles.title: The Unbroken Glass: Bab al-Mandab and the risk of asymmetric escalation
articles.summary: Alliances are drafted for contingencies their signatories hope will remain theoretical. The Makkah Joint Defense Agreement – concluded in August by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan – was one such instrument, yet early this week, less than two months after it was signed, the three states announced the activation of...
articles.body: The Unbroken Glass: Bab al-Mandab and the risk of asymmetric escalation in International Shipping News 22/10/2026 Alliances are drafted for contingencies their signatories hope will remain theoretical. The Makkah Joint Defense Agreement – concluded in August by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan – was one such instrument, yet early this week, less than two months after it was signed, the three states announced the activation of its collective deterrence measures. What set it in motion was not an invasion, nor the act of a rival state, but a campaign by a non-state movement based in the northern highlands of Yemen. It may prove the first of many state responses in this particular area. The risk differs from that which markets have watched at Hormuz, a problem of leverage in which any actor able to threaten a narrow gateway can impose costs far beyond its physical power. Bab al-Mandab is where the workaround runs. Saudi loadings at Yanbu, on the Red Sea, rose more than sixfold in March, from roughly 0.8 million barrels per day to about 5 million bpd, once Hormuz was effectively shut. Around 80% of that volume initially moved south through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, until that route was jeopardized by the Houthi campaign launched in July. This presents a different vulnerability – asymmetric escalation – where a limited action by an actor of modest means and loose control draws disproportionate responses from many more powerful ones, none of which intends to engage in a wider war. The asymmetry has three dimensions: of scale, since a narrow act produces broad consequences; of actor, since a movement acts while states and alliances must respond; and of control, since no one involved can ultimately determine where the sequence ends with certainty. The same maritime system has produced this pattern before. In 1956 the crisis at Suez owed little to the quarrel over the canal that started it. Britain, France and Israel each came to the same waterway by a different road, the superpowers were drawn in behind them, and an Egyptian dispute ended as a verdict on the limits of post-war European power. Suez is the best template for what follows, with one difference: the party that began that quarrel was a state that could be negotiated with and pressured. The Houthis are not that. The sequence Houthi missile salvos fired at Israel in March widened over the summer into a campaign that broke the militia’s four-year ceasefire with Saudi Arabia. On 20 July the Houthis declared an embargo on Saudi vessels while indicating that other shipping could pass. Most vessels, reportedly, still pass Bab al-Mandab without incident, but weekly transits through the strait fell from 354 – the highest total since December 2023 – to 269 in the first week of the embargo. In September the campaign changed in kind. Drone strikes on 10 September, which Riyadh attributed to launches from Iraqi territory, damaged pumping stations on the East-West pipeline, the kingdom’s principal export artery since Hormuz was constrained. The line restarted on 22 September at reduced rates. In mid-September the Houthis also reportedly took control of the port of Mocha and Perim Island. Yemeni government forces say they retook Mocha on 5 October, but this is refuted by the Houthis. This is no longer only a maritime problem; it is a national security question for the state targeted. The shoreline is of vital strategic importance. Perim divides the strait’s narrowest point into two lanes, the Large Strait of about 17 kilometers and the Small Strait of 2.5 to 5 kilometers. A position on the island would let the Houthis rely on cheap, replenishable weapons, such as sea mines and explosive drone boats, and could allow them to impose transit fees, as Iran has attempted at Hormuz. So far, the pressure has been selective. That is the asymmetry of scale: inexpensive means, expensive consequences. The actor matters as much as the geography. Iran has helped develop the Houthis’ capabilities, but sponsorship is not traditional command and control. Tehran can enable and influence Houthi action without determining every decision. A sovereign government weighs its territory, economy and diplomatic relationships before it uses force; a non-state movement carries a different ledger. Even if the blockade is a bargaining move rather than a bid for wider war, a bargaining move by one party can become the trigger for another. This is the asymmetry of actor: in 1956 Washington’s financial pressure on the British pound halted the Anglo-French operation against Egypt within days, but no comparable lever exists over a movement in the Yemeni highlands. Why responses compound The Makkah agreement shows the sequence is in motion, at least politically. It went unused for two months while Pakistan and Turkey, which had positioned themselves as mediators in the wider conflict with Iran, weighed their roles. The commitment made on 5 October was an announcement pertaining to collective deterrence measures, not a deployment. No troop numbers or dates have been given, Pakistan’s forces were already in Saudi Arabia in supporting roles, and Turkey’s parliament has yet to ratify the pact, although statements from Islamabad and Ankara on 8 October may define the commitment and accelerate it. Amid such escalation, each response may be proportionate: a defensive deployment is read as preparation for offense, a naval escort as a widening commitment, a commercial diversion as evidence that disruption is permanent. Suez is again the guide. Each of the 1956 participants acted on what looked like a sound reading of its own interests, and the sum was a canal blocked by sunken ships, a disrupted European oil supply and a British prime minister who resigned within months. No one chose the whole. That is the asymmetry of control: each decision is reasonable on its own terms, and their sum is not. The same asymmetry also supplies reasons for restraint. A cheap provocation is expensive to answer, and the stronger parties know it. Saudi Arabia has little appetite for another prolonged confrontation with the Houthis, and Turkey and Pakistan have even less reason to be drawn into direct combat, which is consistent with the supporting roles they have so far described. Suez points the same way: the escalation was bounded within days, and Britain’s prime minister paid with his office for pushing it. Where the cost lands Each workaround has become the next chokepoint. When Hormuz was effectively shut after the war began on 28 February, Middle East crude loadings fell from about 19.4 million barrels per day in February to about 10 million in March, and the Red Sea became the main outlet for Saudi crude. As the Houthi campaign pushed vessels north, away from the southern route, Egypt’s Sumed pipeline, with 2.5 million bpd of capacity, absorbed much of the diversion. Crude is offloaded at the Red Sea end, piped across Egypt and reloaded on the Mediterranean coast. The Suez Canal cannot do that job on its own, because only vessels up to Suezmax size can transit it fully laden, so the largest crude carriers loading on the Red Sea either depend on Sumed or must still pass south through Bab al-Mandab. A barrel rerouted away from one chokepoint inherits the risk of another. The adaptation is not temporary, and Suez set the precedent. When Egypt closed the canal in 1967 it stayed shut until 1975, and shipowners responded by building ever larger tankers that made the long route around the Cape of Good Hope economic. Sumed itself was completed in 1977 as a consequence. The detour became the standard route, and the ships built for it could no longer use the canal fully laden even after it reopened. Vessel tracking shows the same pattern in LNG today. In 2023, about a third of US LNG exports to Asia went through Suez. After mid-January 2024, the trade virtually stopped using the canal, and by 2025 a dominant 88% went via the Cape. The cost of the cascade shows in prices. Brent traded above $108 in mid-September and hovered between $98 and $101 in the first week of October. July price scenarios spanned from roughly $65 under full resolution to about $148 if fighting escalated and Bab al-Mandab were disrupted; some of this is being borne out now. Freight has changed too, as shipowner earnings on a direct Saudi-to-China VLCC voyage passed $1 million a day in September, and the shuttle arrangements then in use lifted the cost of landing a barrel in China to about $26, from around $2 before the conflict. Resilience, in other words, is relative: a bypass that funnels through its own chokepoint is less protective than it looks on a map, so the useful question is how many actors a route depends on. That favors diversified supply and shorter, less contested routes to market. Gulf producers remain indispensable. Atlantic Margin basins are a complement, not a replacement, with constraints of their own but less exposure to a non-state actor able to set off a cascade that no one fully controls. Containment Three conclusions follow. The actor is of limited means and loosely controlled, so deterrence works imperfectly. Responses are individually proportionate and collectively not, so every defensive step alters the calculations of others. And markets can absorb a longer route but have yet to price a cascade. The central case remains a shock without a reset, as rerouting, spare pipeline capacity and longer voyages have so far absorbed the strain. Duration, however, is the variable. The longer the crisis persists, the greater the chance that a shock becomes a reset, as Suez did. Whether the cascade is widening will show first in the energy flows rather than in the communiqués – in Yanbu loadings recovering toward their pre-attack level, in Sumed throughput, and in southbound transits by VLCCs. The Makkah agreement was drafted for a contingency the alliance hoped would not materialize. It has now been invoked; how far it is tested is yet to be seen. Suez ended as a verdict on the limits of power, and Bab al-Mandab may yet deliver another verdict on the limits of control. The glass has not broken, and fatigue, cost and the example of Suez all work to keep it intact. But it has cracked in plain view, and the pressure is spreading through every connection the region has. If it does shatter, it may well be on the rocks of the aptly named Gate of Lamentation. articles.body: Maersk expects full return of shipping services to Suez Canal by March 2027 in International Shipping News 22/10/2026 Denmark-based shipping group A.P. Moller-Maersk expects all its shipping services to return to the Suez Canal by March 2027, according to a statement from the Suez Canal Authority (SCA). The outlook was unveiled during a videoconference between Ossama Rabiee, Chairman and Managing Director of the SCA, and Rabab Boulos, Maersk’s Chief Operating Officer and a member of its executive leadership team. The talks focused on strengthening cooperation and reviewing sailing plans and schedules to accelerate the return of services through the canal. Rabiee reported that Maersk-affiliated vessels made 276 transits through the canal between January and September 2026, with a combined net tonnage of 23.3 million tons. This compared with 146 transits totaling 7 million net tons during the same period in 2025. He described a substantial recovery in Maersk services using the waterway, attributing it to the strategic partnership and longstanding relationship between the two sides. Boulos also credited their cooperation with bringing back a significant number of services and identified the canal as Maersk’s preferred route. On preparations for further returns, Ahmed Hassan, a senior vice president at Maersk who also attended the meeting, said the group continued to revise its sailing schedules to enable more services to pass through the canal in the coming period. Hany El Nady, Maersk’s Chief Group Representative for the Middle East and North Africa, also participated in the talks and said the company was working to accelerate the restoration of all its services through the waterway. Rabiee highlighted the canal’s economic advantages, saying geopolitical developments and their impact on rising fuel prices and freight rates had reinforced its strategic importance. He said the route offered substantial cost savings for very large container ships and greater navigational safety than sailing around the Cape of Good Hope. articles.body: Verde Marine expands bunker fleet in International Shipping News 22/10/2026 Dutch bunker supplier Verde Marine Energy has added more bunker barges to its fleet, expanding its physical bunker operations in the ARA region. The company has added barges to serve customers in Flushing, Ternuezen and Ghent, it said. The company has also added a dedicated barge for HSFO supply. This follows Verde Marine entering an agreement with U.S.-based bunker supplier Sunoco Marine in August to expand bunkering operations in the ARA and the UK. The companies had said then that they would be adding barges, products and supply locations as part of the collaboration. In June, Verde Marine had started supplying marine biofuels, including B100, in the ARA region. The company said that it has since then delivered thousands of metric tonnes of B100 across the region by barge and by truck. articles.body: Panama Canal Reports Growth in Transits and Tonnage in Fiscal Year 2026 in Port News 22/10/2026 The Panama Canal recorded growth in both vessel transits and tonnage in Fiscal Year 2026, which ran from October 2025 through September 2026. The results underscore the waterway’s ability to meet the demand of global maritime trade while continuing to adapt to the effects of El Niño. The Panama Canal presented its FY2026 results today during a call hosted by Anna Milne, Managing Director of Emerging Markets Corporate Research at Bank of America Merrill Lynch. Panama Canal Administrator Ilya Espino de Marotta, Deputy Administrator Miguel Lorenzo, and Vice President of Finance Juan Mojica discussed the canal’s water management strategy and progress on initiatives under its Vision 2025–2035, including the Río Indio Lake Project. Operational Performance The Panama Canal handled 13,951 transits in FY2026, up 4.1% from 13,404 in FY2025. Growth was driven by energy shipping segments and strong containership performance. Tonnage reached 521 million Panama Canal Universal Measurement System (PC/UMS) tons, an increase of 6.5% from 489.2 million PC/UMS tons the previous fiscal year. Vessels transiting the Neopanamax locks accounted for 52.2% of total tonnage, with tonnage through these locks rising 8.2% year over year. This growth reflects the increasing share of larger-capacity vessels using the waterway. The results reflect a sustained recovery in demand, supported in part by shifts in international trade flows. The Panama Canal also maintained a maximum draft of 50 feet throughout the dry season, providing favorable operating conditions for its customers. Total revenue for FY2026 reached B/. 6.6 billion, an increase of 16.6% over the previous fiscal year. These unaudited figures reflect strong financial discipline and will support investment in strategic projects that will shape the future of the canal. “Far from restricting trade flows, the Panama Canal facilitates international maritime trade by providing its customers with a reliable and safe route,” Administrator Espino de Marotta said during the call. Results from FY2026 also highlight the performance and dedication of the canal’s workforce and its ability to deliver strong results in a complex global environment. Last Minute Reservations With water conservation measures proving effective and recent rainfall in the watershed approaching average levels, the Panama Canal announced today, through an Advisory to Shipping, the immediate reinstatement of its Last-Minute Reservation service for vessels using the Panamax locks. The service gives vessels without a reservation an additional opportunity to secure a transit slot when one becomes available and the canal, at its discretion, chooses to offer it. The Panama Canal remains committed to closely monitoring water conditions and rainfall and will promptly communicate any further adjustments as circumstances require. articles.body: Valenciaport presents its Sandbox at PEIC’26 as a tool to bridge the gap between innovation and implementation in Port News 22/10/2026 The 2026 International Port Entrepreneurship Congress (PEIC’26) has kicked off its latest edition, highlighting the growing international interest in port entrepreneurship. Mar Chao, President of the Port Authority of Valencia (PAV), emphasised the importance of innovation as “an essential requirement to continue growing and remain competitive, sustainable and resilient. Mar Chao ha sido la encargada de inaugurar la jornada, junto al director general de la Fundación Valenciaport (FV), Antonio Torregrosa, con sendas intervenciones en las que han puesto en valor un encuentro que reúne a representantes de puertos, startups, corporaciones logísticas e inversores de todo el mundo y se ha convertido en punto de encuentro internacional para la innovación y el emprendimiento portuario. In this context, the President highlighted several initiatives launched by the Port Authority of Valencia that reflect its commitment to applied innovation, particularly the Valenciaport Sandbox. “The Sandbox was created with a simple objective: to enable innovative solutions to be tested in a real-world port environment,” she explained. She also expressed her hope that projects such as this would make “the journey from innovation to implementation faster, more efficient and more valuable for everyone involved.” For his part, Antonio Torregrosa highlighted the strong interest shown by ports, major companies, investors and innovation leaders in taking part in the event. In his view, this demonstrates the emergence of an increasingly large international community that sees open innovation “as a key driver of the future of the maritime and logistics sectors.” More than 45 startups from 12 different countries The discussion, entitled “Opening Perspectives: Enabling Port Innovation and Entrepreneurship”, marked the start of the fourth edition of the congress, bringing together startups from 12 countries in Valencia to showcase their technologies to the port community. Over the course of the two-day event, a total of 20 startups are expected to take to the stage, alongside five selected to compete in the VDS pitch competition, others showcasing their technologies in the new demonstration area at the lake of the City of Arts and Sciences, and 13 taking part in the PEIC Resilience Forum. In total, more than 45 selected startups have gathered in Valencia to share their innovations. The congress, now in its fourth edition at the City of Arts and Sciences, introduces several major new features, including “PEIC Demo on the Lake” and the new, larger Agora Stage. These additions build on the spirit of previous editions: connecting startups, international port companies and institutions, and specialised venture capital investors. PEIC has firmly established itself as a must-attend event on the port innovation calendar. Over the course of the event, Valenciaport serves as a meeting point for ports from Spain and around the world to share common challenges, discover innovative solutions and connect directly with the companies developing them. “That is why events like this are so important. They bring together those who understand the operational challenges facing the sector and those working to address them. This is where partnerships are forged and, in many cases, turn into innovations that deliver tangible impact,” concluded the President of Valenciaport. articles.body: Freightos has signed an agreement with cargo airline mas to expand digital air cargo booking and payment services across Latin America. The partnership will bring mas’s widebody freighter capacity onto the Freightos platform. Freight forwarders will be able to book cargo space in real time and complete payments through an integrated digital system. The planned integration will initially focus on freight forwarders operating in Los Angeles and across Mexico. It will provide access to mas’s dedicated freighter network serving destinations throughout Latin America. Digital bookings and payments in one platform The agreement combines Freightos’ electronic booking capabilities with Freightos Pay, its digital payment solution. Once the integration is available, freight forwarders will be able to search for capacity, make bookings and arrange payments through the same platform. The service aims to reduce manual booking procedures and simplify payment arrangements. Flexible payment options are also expected to help forwarders manage cash flow when securing cargo space. “By pairing mas’s dedicated widebody network with Freightos Pay, we are replacing administrative friction with instant execution,” said Pablo Pinillos, CEO of Freightos. Expanding access to Latin American cargo capacity The partnership will give mas another digital distribution channel for its freighter services. It will also provide freight forwarders with additional options for booking main-deck cargo capacity on routes connecting North America and Latin America. According to Eduardo Cedilli, Senior Manager, Sales at mas, the integration will help the airline reach more freight forwarders while simplifying its booking and payment processes. The companies expect the partnership to support faster bookings and improve access to available capacity. However, Freightos has not announced a launch date for the integration or specified how many aircraft will be included.

The Philippines and Taiwan have repeatedly complained about Chinese activities designed to pressure the countries without direct confrontation. Carino III, Manila’s deputy chief of mission in Washington, told a seminar this “pragmatic and practical approach” with Taiwan was necessary to protect mutual interests in the Bashi Channel between Taiwan and the Philippines. Speaking to Washington’s Center for a New American Security, Carino linked cable security to South China Sea tensions, but did not mention China by name. He said security of undersea cables was vital given that they carried nearly all intercontinental data flows “and that 60-67% of cyber incidents happen in our region.” “These are very important features that should be protected, so much so that we are exploring deeper cooperation with our friends in Taiwan,” Carino said, adding that the Philippines was doing so “notwithstanding our one China policy.” He said the Philippines and Taiwan were exploring “practical and more pragmatic approaches in cooperation, including knowledge-sharing and capacity building” and added: “We see this cooperation leading towards … addressing the gray-zone issues in our part of the world.” China warned the Philippines that it should “strictly adhere to the one-China Principle with real actions” and sent Taiwan a similar message, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Thursday. Asked if this cooperation could include joint patrols or accountability for vessels that disrupt communications, Carino said he did not have details, but said: “I’m sure that this is a constantly evolving cooperation, and some of the things that you mentioned may be actually coming to fruition.” Taipei has stepped up efforts to protect undersea communications links, which are vital to the island’s connections to the rest of the world, after several incidents involving cables and China-linked vessels. This month, the Philippines’ coast guard said it had deployed its largest vessel and an aircraft to challenge a Chinese research ship operating off northern Batanes province near undersea cable corridors . At the same seminar, Andrea Yang, Taiwan’s deputy representative in Washington, referred to the jailing in Taiwan of a Chinese ship captain over damage to an undersea cable. She said Taiwan would put more resources into developing unmanned systems to improve maritime surveillance. REUTERS/Ahmed Jadallah By Salma El Wardany Oct 22, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Saudi Arabia is in talks with foreign governments to give state-owned Aramco access to their strategic oil storage, as the kingdom seeks to make its supplies to customers more resilient during disruptions, Chief Executive Officer Amin Nasser said. The move follows a flurry of attacks by Yemen’s Houthis on key Saudi infrastructure, including drone strikes that shut down its most important pipeline for several days in September. On Wednesday , attacks on Aramco’s Shaybah oil field and Dammam airport each killed two people, according to Saudi authorities. Brent crude climbed above $112 a barrel on Thursday as the violence heightened concerns about further disruptions to Saudi supplies. “Commercial storage available through partners is limited. The larger capacity lies in what we call strategic storage owned by governments,” Nasser said in an interview with Al Arabiya on Thursday. “The Ministry of Energy is working with its counterparts in other countries to make strategic storage available for Aramco.” The company already holds commercial oil storage in South Korea, Japan, the Netherlands and Egypt’s Mediterranean export hub of Sidi Kerir. “We have maintained these overseas inventories for many years, but we are working to expand them, particularly in Asia,” Nasser said. Aramco wants to double its overseas capacity, Nasser said, without giving a timetable for the expansion or disclosing current capacity. The push forms part of a broader effort to reinforce Saudi Arabia’s infrastructure and export options during the regional crisis. Aramco currently has three main export corridors — the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb, and Sidi Kerir on the Mediterranean. The conflict prompted the company to begin engineering studies to increase its capacity to move crude from the Persian Gulf in the east to the Red Sea in the west to 10 million barrels a day from 7 million, alongside work on other routes, Nasser said. “We did not wait for the crisis to end,” Nasser said. Building resilience requires “decades of investment and preparation.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. The US State Department plans to withdraw family members from a number of other US missions in the region, US officials told Reuters. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis struck several targets on Wednesday with at least one person killed and eight more wounded at a civilian airport in Dammam, and two people killed in a drone attack on a Saudi oil field. articles.title: OneSubsea and oil & gas giants are unlocking deeper waters with all-electric subsea tech
articles.summary: Out with hydraulics, in with electric: OneSubsea, TotalEnergies, Equinor, BP, and Chevron have tested all-electric tech at depths up to 3,000 meters.
articles.body: Technology & Innovation October 22, 2026 · 2 hours ago OneSubsea and oil & gas giants are unlocking deeper waters with all-electric subsea tech Out with hydraulics, in with electric: OneSubsea, TotalEnergies, Equinor, BP, and Chevron have tested all-electric tech at depths up to 3,000 meters. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Brazilian waters served as testing ground for all-electric subsea technology project targeting deepwater fields down to 3,000 meters Source: OneSubsea Pushing deeper into offshore frontiers, OneSubsea, a joint venture backed by SLB, Aker Solutions and Subsea7, has cleared a critical path for deepwater development through a joint industry project with France’s TotalEnergies, Norway’s Equinor, the UK’s BP, and the U.S.-headquartered Chevron to master all-electric subsea technology designed to operate 3,000 meters below the surface. OneSubsea has completed the Brazil All-Electric Joint Industry Project (JIP) , a collaboration with TotalEnergies, Equinor, BP, and Chevron, supported through the National Petroleum Agency (ANP) research and development regulation, to advance fully electric subsea production technologies for applications at water depths of up to 3,000 meters. The subsea player emphasizes that electrification can create new options for designing and operating future deepwater fields by replacing hydraulic actuation with electric systems and connecting subsea equipment, well completion technology, topside controls, and digital capabilities. The Brazilian project qualified electric components and control systems for deepwater applications and demonstrated an integrated architecture extending electrification beyond the subsea tree, connecting subsea production equipment with electric well completion technology, topside controls, and digital capabilities. Representatives from the participating companies recently gathered at the OneSubsea manufacturing facility in São José dos Pinhais, Brazil, to celebrate the completion of the project through technical presentations, demonstrations of subsea and downhole all-electric technologies, and a tour of the facility where electrified subsea equipment will be assembled. Darcy Ryan , Product Manager at OneSubsea, commented: “Completing this project is an important step toward expanding the role of fully electric technology in future deepwater developments. By working closely with operators to define requirements and qualify the technology, we are creating new possibilities to simplify subsea infrastructure while providing greater control, monitoring and access to data.” As subsea developments move into deeper water and increasingly complex environments, OneSubsea points out that operators are looking for new ways to simplify infrastructure, improve control, and create greater flexibility in how future fields are designed. Since traditional hydraulic systems require extensive distribution infrastructure to operate subsea equipment, adding complexity as developments extend farther from existing facilities, the company believes that this is where all-electric can make a difference. “Conventional subsea production systems use hydraulic pressure to actuate valves and chokes, requiring hydraulic distribution infrastructure across the field. All-electric technology replaces hydraulic actuation with electric motors, eliminating the need for hydraulic fluids and reducing associated infrastructure,” elaborated OneSubsea. The firm explains that the Brazilian project demonstrates how electrification can move beyond individual components toward an integrated production architecture that connects subsea equipment, well completion technology, topside controls, and digital systems. Aside from qualifying components for applications at depths of up to 3,000 meters, the project pinpointed interfaces with newly developed and qualified SLB electric completion technologies. OneSubsea underlined: “A purpose-built master control station connects the subsea equipment with topside control and digital systems, enabling an integrated approach to monitoring and operating the production system. “This architecture can simplify field layouts and reduce overall system complexity while giving operators greater flexibility when developing longer tiebacks, more remote fields, and increasingly autonomous operations.” The company states that the completion of the project builds on more than 15 years of experience in subsea electrification and more than 5 million operating hours with electrified subsea systems. The firm’s all-electric portfolio is advancing along two complementary paths, with all-electric subsea production technology moving toward commercial deployment through Equinor’s Fram Sør project in Norway, which includes 12 all-electric subsea trees . articles.title: Global shipbuilding boom moves into overdrive
articles.summary: The global shipbuilding boom is gathering pace, with orderbooks surpassing their previous 2008 peak, Chinese yards tightening their grip on the market and tanker owners increasingly turning to inexperienced builders to secure delivery slots. New figures from BIMCO put the global orderbook at 203.2m compensated gross...
articles.body: Shipyards Global shipbuilding boom moves into overdrive Sam Chambers October 22, 2026 1 644 1 minute read Hengli Hengli The global shipbuilding boom is gathering pace, with orderbooks surpassing their previous 2008 peak, Chinese yards tightening their grip on the market and tanker owners increasingly turning to inexperienced builders to secure delivery slots. New figures from BIMCO put the global orderbook at 203.2m compensated gross tonnes (cgt) at the start of September, up 13% year-on-year and just below May’s all-time high of 210.4m cgt. China captured 74% of new cgt contracted over the preceding 12 months, lifting its share of the global orderbook to 64%, against South Korea’s 19% and Japan’s 6%. Containerships account for 30% of tonnage on order and 68% of the past year’s growth. BIMCO calculates that Chinese yards hold orders equivalent to 4.2 years of recent peak annual production, compared with 1.9 years in South Korea and 1.7 in Japan. Chinese yards are scheduled to deliver a record 44m cgt in 2028, nearly twice the 22.7m cgt delivered in 2025 “Chinese yards are scheduled to deliver a record 44m cgt in 2028, nearly twice the 22.7m cgt delivered in 2025,” said BIMCO chief shipping analyst Niels Rasmussen, warning that the necessary capacity expansion risks leaving yards underutilised when contracting eventually slows. The squeeze is already bringing new shipbuilders into the tanker market. Veson Nautical reports that 51 vessels have been ordered at newly entering yards this year, up 34% from 2025. Eleven of the 16 yards identified are Chinese. The standout is Hengli Shipbuilding, which delivered its first vessel in 2024 and now holds an extraordinary 495-ship orderbook valued at $46bn. “Owners’ willingness to place orders at yards without an established tanker track record likely reflects capacity constraints at established tanker-building yards,” observed Veson analyst Rebecca Galanopoulos. Yet, despite the rush, tanker newbuilding prices remain surprisingly affordable relative to historical peaks. Broker Affinity noted in a recent research note that VLCC newbuilding prices are still 20% to 25% below their 2008 highs in nominal terms, despite today’s unprecedented tanker earnings. Adjusted for inflation, a $160m VLCC in 2008 would cost roughly $250m today, nearly double current prices. Affinity argued that Hengli’s enormous capacity injection has restrained prices, although disappearing early delivery slots and shortages of engines and pumps could soon trigger another upward move. articles.body: Greater China Shipyards China adds new state-owned shipbuilding player in Guangzhou Adis Ajdin October 22, 2026 0 292 1 minute read Guangzhou SASAC Guangzhou SASAC Guangzhou has formally launched a new state-owned maritime industrial group as the southern Chinese shipbuilding hub looks to expand its manufacturing capacity and bring more of the industry’s supply chain under local ownership. Guangzhou Marine Equipment Group, established with registered capital of RMB2bn ($300m), has begun operations following an unveiling ceremony this week. The company is wholly owned by Guangzhou Industrial Investment Holding Group, with the municipal government as its ultimate shareholder. It was incorporated in July but has now formally launched its operations and signed a series of cooperation agreements. The new group has joined forces with China State Shipbuilding Corporation-controlled Guangzhou Shipyard International (GSI) and Huangpu Wenchong, as well as COSCO Shipping Specialized Carriers, marine technology company SEAHI Robotics and the Guangzhou branch of China Classification Society. The move is intended to strengthen Guangzhou’s position in shipbuilding by combining local manufacturing assets with investment and maritime services. The group will draw on businesses involved in marine propulsion, heavy engineering and shipboard equipment, including Guangzhou Diesel Engine Factory, while expanding into vessel retrofits, equipment maintenance, industrial park development, leasing and inspection services. Guangzhou Marine Equipment Group has set a target of reaching about $3.9bn in business scale by 2030, according to local government-backed reporting. The launch comes alongside a major expansion of the city’s shipbuilding infrastructure. Guangzhou is developing a new marine equipment manufacturing and shipbuilding base at Longxue North in Nansha, involving investment of approximately $1.09bn. The project was launched in September and is being developed separately from the new group’s establishment. GSI is lined up to operate the facility, which is expected to be completed in 2029. Guangzhou Marine Equipment Group is also lined up to participate in the development, although its financial commitment has not been disclosed. The latest move follows a series of investments by Guangzhou’s established shipbuilders to deal with bulging orderbooks. GSI recently signed an agreement with China Railway Shanhaiguan Bridge Group to outsource hull block production, adding manufacturing capacity outside the traditional shipbuilding supply chain. The yard has also been expanding its physical footprint, with new facilities planned at Xiaohudao and Longxue North as construction slots stretch towards 2030. articles.title: A new world order emerges in LNG shipping
articles.summary: The world’s LNG trading map is undergoing its biggest upheaval in years, with the near-paralysis of Gulf exports redirecting cargoes across oceans, forcing Asian buyers towards alternative suppliers and pushing European gas prices to their highest levels since 2022. While gas prices approach $30 per million British...
articles.body: Gas A new world order emerges in LNG shipping Sam Chambers October 22, 2026 0 358 3 minutes read Teo Malnar Teo Malnar The world’s LNG trading map is undergoing its biggest upheaval in years, with the near-paralysis of Gulf exports redirecting cargoes across oceans, forcing Asian buyers towards alternative suppliers and pushing European gas prices to their highest levels since 2022. While gas prices approach $30 per million British thermal units, LNG carrier spot earnings remain remarkably weak, with the Baltic Exchange assessing the US Gulf-Europe route at just $21,200 a day last week. Nearly eight months into the Hormuz crisis, oil exporters have found ways around the chokepoint. Kpler estimates that non-Iranian Middle Eastern oil flows, including alternative routes, recovered to prewar levels last week. LNG remains a different proposition, with Qatar unable to replicate the pipelines and offshore transfers that have restored much of the region’s crude trade. Vortexa recorded just five confirmed LNG carrier transits of Hormuz last week, against a four-week average of 12. Only two were laden outbound voyages. Ras Laffan loaded five cargoes totalling 400,000 tonnes. Kpler identified 13 Qatari LNG loadings during October 1-13, but only four ships were broadcasting active AIS signals. The remaining nine were verified through satellite imagery, tug tracking and other intelligence. The Al Kharsaah, carrying Qatari LNG towards Poland via the Red Sea, came under fire from a small boat in the Gulf of Aden on October 17. Its armed security team returned warning shots, forcing the attackers to retreat. The voyage could deliver Europe’s first Qatari cargo since April. The disruption is now being measured in cancelled contracts as well as missing ships. Italy’s Edison has received force majeure notices covering 35 Qatari LNG cargoes, equivalent to 4.6bn cu m of gas, with deliveries suspended until early December. Damage inflicted on two liquefaction trains at Ras Laffan in March has also removed 12.8m tonnes of annual production capacity, with repairs potentially taking years. The US is meanwhile cementing its position as the indispensable swing supplier. American terminals dispatched 2.5m tonnes across 36 cargoes last week, according to Vortexa, while official US figures show exports surged 23% in the first half of 2026. There is an irony in the American resurgence. QatarEnergy owns 70% of Golden Pass in Texas, where an expanding export operation is helping diversify its supply portfolio beyond the troubled Gulf. Europe is capturing an increasing share of Atlantic supply. S&P Global data shows Europe and Turkey received 76 of the 143 US LNG cargoes delivered in September. Egypt has also become a major destination, taking 14 American cargoes during the month as declining domestic production increases its dependence on imported gas. The reshuffle is particularly visible in India. Oman, whose LNG terminals sit outside Hormuz, displaced the US as India’s largest supplier in September. Kpler recorded 590,000 tonnes arriving from Oman, compared with 350,000 tonnes from Nigeria and 340,000 tonnes from the US. Qatar, once India’s dominant supplier, managed just 100,000 tonnes. Not all Asian buyers are responding alike. Indian LNG imports were 7% higher year-on-year in September despite elevated prices. China, Japan and South Korea have proved more reluctant to chase expensive spot cargoes. Japan’s major utilities held 2.64m tonnes of LNG in inventory earlier this month, their highest stockpile since December 2023. South Korea is increasingly relying on coal generation, with Kpler projecting available coal plant utilisation of 63.5% in November and December. IFCHOR Galbraiths calculates that South Korean coal imports rose 14% year-on-year during January-September, while Japan’s increased 8%. China’s September LNG imports fell to 5.2m tonnes, according to Kpler, as weaker industrial demand and growing pipeline supplies reduced its need for seaborne gas. Europe has less flexibility. Gas storage was just 74.6% full this week, nearly 15 percentage points below its five-year seasonal average, with Germany at around 61%. A cold winter would intensify competition for Atlantic cargoes, particularly as the EU prepares to end remaining Russian LNG imports from January 1. Stronger European demand for US gas has shortened average Atlantic voyages, releasing vessels back into the market more quickly and depressing tonne-mile demand. Baltic Exchange assessments last week put the US Gulf-Japan route at $49,000 a day, more than twice the equivalent European route. Fleet expansion adds another complication. Flex LNG estimates the global orderbook at approximately 285 vessels, equivalent to 37% of the existing fleet, with around 95 deliveries expected next year. Beyond the immediate crisis, another geographical shift is gathering momentum. LNG Canada’s September investment decision to double capacity to 28m tonnes annually reinforces the emergence of a Pacific export corridor offering Asian customers shorter voyages than traditional Atlantic suppliers. Meanwhile, Europe’s Russian LNG ban could force Arctic cargoes towards more distant Asian destinations, creating fresh shipping demand but also logistical and sanctions-related complications. The emerging picture for LNG shipping is one of greater geographical diversification, increasingly unpredictable cargo movements and an uncomfortable mismatch between the price of gas and the value of carrying it. A delegation from ANPG, led by Administrator Ana Miala , together with representatives from TotalEnergies, Petronas, and Sonangol visited the OneSubsea facilities in Johor, Republic of Malaysia, at the end of last month to monitor the manufacturing of equipment that integrates the subsea production system (SPS) of the Kaminho project. Visit to OneSubsea's facilities was made to check on the progress of the subsea production system for Kaminho; Courtesy of ANPG During the visit, the delegation confirmed the planned schedule for the arrival in Angola, starting in 2027, of the equipment currently in production at OneSubsea's facilities in Malaysia. Before its offshore installation, this equipment will be tested by Angolan OneSubsea teams at the company's testing facilities in Sonils, Luanda. Among the components being manufactured are 13 subsea Christmas trees, with a focus on safety, quality, and delivery of said equipment within the planned deadlines. The execution of the Kaminho project has already exceeded 50%. The Kaminho project's subsea production system will be installed at a depth greater than 1,500 meters and will connect the wells of the Cameia reservoir to the system of pipelines that carry hydrocarbons to the FPSO Kaminho to allow them to be treated and separated into water, gas, and crude oil. Located in Block 20/11, about 100 kilometers off the Angolan coast, Kaminho is scheduled to come online in 2028. articles.body: Americas Asia Europe Middle East Operations Regulatory Tankers US sanctions net widens to shipping agents and lawyers Sam Chambers October 22, 2026 0 760 1 minute read Washington.org Washington.org Washington has widened its crackdown on Iran’s shadow fleet, sanctioning a Greek-Panamanian law firm, shipping agents in Singapore and Dubai, and nine vessels in a move targeting the service providers behind Tehran’s commodity exports. Announcing the measures yesterday, the US Treasury said Karnakis and Karnakis had established corporate structures for shipowners moving hundreds of millions of dollars worth of Iranian oil, LPG, petrochemicals and steel. Five individuals linked to the practice have also been designated. Among the companies blacklisted is Roxette Maritime Shipping and Trading, the Panama- and Greece-based manager of seven Panama-flagged bulk carriers and general cargo ships. Treasury identified Anemos, Gloris and Pride as having carried Iranian-origin cargoes over the past year. The group’s other designated ships are Destiny, Flamingo 1, Harmony and Prince. Singapore-based Amigoz Singapore was sanctioned for acting as port agent for a shipment of Iranian light crude and providing bunkering services to the shadow fleet tanker Zixuan. Treasury also linked the company to networks associated with Iranian shipping figure Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani. Dubai-based Whales Shipping Line was designated for supporting Amigoz and acting as shipping agent for a company accused of arranging Iranian petrochemical purchases. Its two UAE-flagged support vessels, Whales Diamond and Whales Pearl, were also blacklisted. The action forms part of Operation Economic Outcast, launched in August, which is intended to cut Iran off from international financial and shipping services. articles.body: Dry Cargo Europe Tankers Tufton rides stronger markets with fresh tanker and bulker deals Adis Ajdin October 22, 2026 0 211 1 minute read Brian Kushner / Marine Traffic Brian Kushner / Marine Traffic London-listed Tufton Assets has secured higher-paying employment across its tanker and dry bulk fleet, with two MR product tankers extended for another year and further charter renewals in the pipeline. The charterer of the 2016-built Catherine Grace and Madelyn Grace exercised options in October to extend both vessels’ employment by 12 months at rates above their previous firm periods, the ship investment company said in its third-quarter update. The latest extensions add to a string of chartering moves during the third quarter, when the company secured improved terms for three vessels and fixed two handysize bulkers on new arrangements. Among the latest dry bulk fixtures, the ultramax African Inspiration has been extended for six to eight months from early October at a substantially higher rate, while the handysize Lucilia C has started a new seven- to nine-month charter following the expiry of its previous employment in September. The moves follow Tufton’s September fixing of the MR product tanker Mia Grace at $39,000 per day for 12 to 14 months, an 81% jump from its previous $21,500 daily rate. The company also secured more than $15,000 per day for handysize bulker Amilyn and converted the index-linked charter of sistership Staithes to a fixed $19,000 per day for the fourth quarter. The wider chartering activity comes as Tufton benefits from stronger tanker and dry bulk markets. The company said disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, coupled with reduced availability of compliant tankers, had helped lift freight rates, while grain, iron ore and bauxite demand supported dry bulk earnings. Tufton’s fleet currently comprises 21 vessels, including eight product tankers, two chemical tankers and 11 bulk carriers. The company’s net asset value rose to $1.63 per share at the end of September, representing a 5% total return for the quarter. Earlier this year, Tufton expanded its dry bulk exposure with the $33m acquisition of two Japanese-built handysize vessels, which entered the fleet in April. Further chartering opportunities are approaching, with existing contracts for three tankers and four bulkers due to expire in the coming months. The company said it was assessing the market for new employment to take advantage of stronger rates. articles.title: COSCO Shipping Ports: What is driving its overseas terminal growth?
articles.summary: COSCO Shipping Ports’ overseas terminal portfolio is outperforming its wider network in 2026, although the headline figures conceal significant differences between individual facilities. According to the latest throughput figures reported by Container News, the company’s overseas terminals, excluding Container...
articles.body: COSCO Shipping Ports’ overseas terminal portfolio is outperforming its wider network in 2026, although the headline figures conceal significant differences between individual facilities. According to the latest throughput figures reported by Container News , the company’s overseas terminals, excluding Container Terminal Tollerort (CTT), handled 31.48 million TEUs during January–September, an increase of 18.9% year on year. This compares with 8.5% growth across the company’s reported monthly throughput portfolio, which reached 93.91 million TEUs over the same period. Overseas terminals also recorded a 20.7% increase in September alone. The figures indicate that international operations are contributing significantly to the group’s expansion. However, strong gains at some facilities contrast with substantial declines elsewhere, making terminal-level performance essential to understanding the broader trend. Suez leads in volume, Chancay in percentage growth The company’s official monthly throughput statistics reveal sharply contrasting performances across its international portfolio. Terminal Jan–Sep 2026 YoY change Suez Canal Container Terminal 4.70 million TEUs +17.3% Piraeus Container Terminal 3.09 million TEUs +1.7% Euromax Terminal Rotterdam 1.66 million TEUs −5.5% CSP Abu Dhabi Terminal 540,700 TEUs −55.3% CSP Chancay Terminal 341,400 TEUs +47.3% Source: COSCO Shipping Ports, monthly throughput statistics, September 2026. Chancay recorded the fastest percentage growth among these facilities, with throughput increasing 47.3% during the nine-month period. However, its relatively small volume base limits its contribution to the portfolio’s overall expansion. Suez presents a different picture. Its 17.3% growth was recorded on a much larger operational base, representing approximately 693,000 additional TEUs compared with the corresponding period of 2025. By comparison, Chancay’s increase amounted to approximately 110,000 TEUs. This distinction is important: percentage growth highlights momentum, while absolute volume changes provide a clearer indication of which terminals contribute most to overall expansion. Piraeus recorded a comparatively modest 1.7% increase over nine months, despite stronger September growth of 15.3%. The latest monthly improvement is notable, but further data will be needed to determine whether it represents a sustained trend. Abu Dhabi exposes the uneven performance The most significant negative development among the selected facilities comes from CSP Abu Dhabi Terminal. Throughput declined 55.3% to approximately 541,000 TEUs during January–September, compared with around 1.21 million TEUs in the corresponding period of 2025. This represents a reduction of approximately 670,000 TEUs, almost equivalent to the additional volume recorded at Suez over the same period. The decline is particularly relevant because it illustrates how individual terminals can move in sharply different directions despite strong overall portfolio growth. In its first-half results, reported by Container News , COSCO Shipping Ports attributed Abu Dhabi’s weaker performance to geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. The latest statistics show that the terminal’s cumulative decline deepened from 44.3% at the end of June to 55.3% by September. Euromax Terminal Rotterdam also recorded weaker activity, with throughput falling 5.5% during the nine months. These contrasting performances highlight the importance of assessing overseas expansion at the individual terminal level, rather than assuming that strong portfolio growth reflects consistent conditions across all markets. Does higher throughput mean higher profitability? The company’s financial results provide another perspective on its operational development. According to COSCO Shipping Ports’ official 2026 interim results , revenue increased 12.3% to US$905.3 million during the first half of the year. Profit though, attributable to equity holders rose 28.5% to US$233.7 million. Gross profit increased 9.3% to US$239.5 million, although the gross profit margin declined from approximately 27.2% to 26.5%. The figures demonstrate why throughput growth and financial performance should be assessed separately. COSCO Shipping Ports operates through a combination of controlling and non-controlling interests. Consequently, an increase in total containers handled does not necessarily translate proportionately into consolidated revenue or profit attributable to shareholders. The first-half results also reported a 7% increase in equity throughput to 24.49 million TEUs. However, these financial results cover January–June, whereas the latest terminal-level throughput statistics extend through September. They therefore cannot establish how much of the subsequent overseas growth has contributed to earnings. There is also a reporting distinction between the company’s interim results and its monthly throughput statistics. The monthly dataset excludes QPI and CTT, resulting in a different reporting scope. Consequently, the two sets of aggregate throughput figures should not be combined when calculating quarterly changes. What the figures reveal about COSCO’s international portfolio The latest results show that overseas growth is neither uniform nor driven by a single terminal. Suez contributes substantial additional volumes and Chancay continues expanding from a smaller base. Piraeus has recorded stronger recent monthly performance despite limited cumulative growth. At the same time, Abu Dhabi and Euromax demonstrate that significant declines can occur within an otherwise expanding international portfolio. For COSCO Shipping Ports, the commercial challenge is to convert this uneven operating performance into sustainable financial returns across terminals with different ownership structures, market conditions and growth prospects. Subsequent financial disclosures will provide a clearer indication of whether stronger international throughput is translating into improved profitability. COSCO’s overseas expansion is gaining momentum. But the more revealing measure is where additional containers are being handled, where volumes are being lost and how those differences affect the group’s financial performance.
takeaways: COSCO Shipping Ports’ overseas terminal portfolio is outperforming its wider network in 2026, although the headline figures conceal significant differences between individual facilities.

Auto volumes of 208,280 units were down 2.9% year-to-date, with the tariff impact on the automotive sector partially offset by an increase in diverted units from Canada due to congestion. The NWSA noted strong interest from beneficial cargo owners in the gateway’s consistent rail service, particularly low rail dwell times. Evergreen’s HTW service will resume Tacoma calls in late October for 13 weekly voyages, providing exporters with an additional direct ocean service option during peak reefer season, connecting the gateway to key Asian markets and supporting equipment availability and agricultural export capacity. articles.title: US waives new Russia-related tariffs of up to 500%
articles.summary: The White House has waived new sanctions-related import duties targeting Russia and countries involved in Russian energy trade, following an executive order issued on October 16, 2026. The decision concerns measures introduced under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which was signed into...
articles.body: The White House has waived new sanctions-related import duties targeting Russia and countries involved in Russian energy trade, following an executive order issued on October 16, 2026. The decision concerns measures introduced under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which was signed into law on September 18. The legislation provides for additional tariffs of up to 500% on goods originating in Russia. However, the administration has used its authority under the law to waive the new duties on national interest grounds. The tariffs had been scheduled to take effect on October 18, 2026. New tariff measures placed on hold The Graham Act establishes several trade measures targeting Russia and certain countries involved in Russian energy purchases. These include additional duties of up to 500% on Russian-origin imports. The legislation also provides for tariffs of up to 100% on goods from certain countries purchasing Russian oil and natural gas or facilitating the evasion of related sanctions. However, the executive order waives the application of these measures. The waiver does not repeal the legislation or remove other US sanctions against Russia. It means the new penalties covered by the decision are not currently being applied. The administration retains the authority to reconsider the waiver and implement the measures in the future. Implications for international trade The decision is relevant to importers, freight forwarders and logistics companies handling international shipments affected by US trade restrictions. The proposed duties could significantly increase import costs if implemented, particularly for goods originating in Russia and shipments from countries covered by the legislation. For now, the waiver prevents the new tariff measures from taking effect. However, companies must continue to comply with other applicable sanctions, customs requirements and trade restrictions. The White House has cited US national interests as the basis for its decision. The executive order leaves open the possibility of future changes, making the implementation of the Graham Act an important development for businesses involved in international trade.

articles.body: Ports of Stockholm has inaugurated a new port facility at Stockholm Norvik Port designed for the efficient loading of crushed rock aggregates onto bulk carriers, enabling large volumes of material generated during the port’s original construction to be shipped by sea to infrastructure projects across the Baltic Sea region. The facility, built for NCC Industry and consisting of two pile-supported jetties capable of accommodating large bulk carriers, was officially inaugurated on October 16, though shipments had already begun in response to strong market demand. The removal of the stockpiled crushed rock will progressively free up significant areas within Stockholm Norvik Port, providing the foundation for new businesses and marking the starting point for NCC Industry’s planned business and logistics park. The initiative strengthens Stockholm Norvik’s position as a key logistics hub for Swedish imports and exports, complementing its role as Sweden’s newest modern RoRo and container port serving the country’s largest consumer market. Johan Wallén, Chief Commercial Officer at Ports of Stockholm, described the new facility as an important step in the port’s development, enabling more efficient aggregate shipments while unlocking valuable port space for new commercial activity. He highlighted the strategic location and extensive development areas as creating favourable conditions for businesses requiring efficient logistics solutions, with further development of the area to be pursued in partnership with NCC Industry. The facility also opens new opportunities to ship aggregates to additional markets beyond the Baltic Sea region.

One of their main developments is @ILO, a digital twin system that supports groupage cargo handling. The technology helps DACHSER manage cargo handling processes through digital information. It also supports greater visibility across logistics operations. DACHSER expects to have the system in place at 14 locations across Europe by the end of 2026. The @ILO project received the German Logistics Award in 2023. It also won the European Logistics Association Award in early 2026. Over the next three years, the research teams will explore new ways to use artificial intelligence, robotics and digital tools in logistics. “The DACHSER Enterprise Lab, which marries scientific research with practical application, has proven its worth. Over the next three years, we will be focusing on digital solutions, artificial intelligence, and robotics,” said Stefan Hohm, Chief Development Officer at DACHSER. The research will focus on practical applications for DACHSER’s groupage network and wider supply chain operations. Through the partnership, DACHSER aims to turn new technologies into solutions that support its logistics network and improve daily operations.

articles.body: Houston Ship Channel Cargo Volumes Rise as Exports, Steel Imports Surge Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 21, 2026 Copyright Mariusz/AdobeStock Trade activity across the Houston Ship Channel region continued to expand in August and September 2026, with strong growth in foreign cargo exports, vessel traffic, container throughput and steel imports, according to Port Houston's latest Monthly Trade & Market Report. The Houston Ship Channel region handled 22.3 million short tons of foreign cargo in August, an 18% increase from 18.9 million tons in August 2025. Exports drove the growth, rising 24% to 17.8 million tons, while imports remained essentially unchanged at 4.55 million tons. Through the first eight months of 2026, regional foreign cargo totaled 177.9 million tons, up 15% from 154.3 million tons during the corresponding period in 2025. Export tonnage increased 21% to 143.2 million tons, while imports declined 4% to 34.6 million tons. The increase in cargo movement was reflected in vessel traffic. Deep-draft vessel transits totaled 1,596 in September, up 9% year over year, while barge transits increased 11% to 18,819. Year-to-date deep-draft transits reached 14,062, an 8% increase, while barge movements totaled 168,346, up 7%. At Port Houston's public terminals, September container throughput increased 11% to 376,419 TEUs, supported by a 16% increase in loaded imports to 174,189 TEUs. Loaded exports increased 2% to 132,009 TEUs. Through September, total container volume reached 3.35 million TEUs, up 2% year over year. Loaded imports increased 6%, while loaded exports declined 1%. Steel was another standout cargo category. Port Houston handled 581,035 tons of steel in September, a 157% increase from 226,474 tons a year earlier and its strongest monthly steel performance since May 2022. Steel imports accounted for 539,993 tons, an increase of 181%. Despite the sharp monthly gains, year-to-date steel tonnage was up just 1%, reflecting more moderate growth across the first nine months. Overall cargo tonnage at Port Houston's public terminals increased 15% in September to 4.88 million tons, bringing year-to-date volume to 42.37 million tons, up 2%. The report also noted growth through August in containerized imports of apparel and accessories, up 27%; resins and plastics, up 11%; and machinery, appliances and electronics, up 9%. "Behind every shipment are the people and businesses that keep our economy moving," said Charlie Jenkins, CEO of Port Houston. "At the end of the day, our purpose is simple: to support jobs and drive economic prosperity across our region."
