Photo credit: James MacDonald/COAST. A machine learning-driven web app providing whale and dolphin IDs from hydrophone recordings will represent Canada at the Grand Finale of international competition Ocean Hackathon 10. The winning project was chosen during the Victoria edition of 48-hour innovation sprint Ocean Hackathon 10 this past weekend, hosted by COAST, an initiative of the South Island Prosperity Partnership (SIPP), Greater Victoria's economic development alliance. Regional editions were simultaneously convened in twelve cities and nine countries around the world. Produced by Campus Mondial de la Mer, the international competition brings together marine science and digital innovation in a format designed to inspire and engage emerging ocean entrepreneurs. Participants gain access to vast marine databases and receive guidance from experienced mentors and industry professionals while developing their projects. They then pitch their prototypes to a panel of judges. This year, 17 participating university students in the Victoria edition (the only one held in Canada) were assigned to four groups to help solve ocean data challenges. The winning app was developed by B.C. university students Olivia Whitelaw, Grace Bertozzi, Pranav Rajesh Krishnan, Jossie Yan and Leanne Farmer. Dubbed Sea Who's Calling , it is a prototype monitoring tool with potential for global application. Its primary goal is to support decision-making for the Royal Canadian Navy when planning exercises to mitigate potential impacts on marine mammals, while also providing accurate data on each type of whale or dolphin that may be in the area. Initial trials show Sea Who's Calling can classify marine mammals with a higher degree of accuracy than its closest competitor, while also being able to discern and distinguish more species. In testing on expert-labelled recordings from Ocean Networks Canada, it outperformed leading bioacoustics models from Google DeepMind, Cornell's K. Lisa Yang Center for Conservation Bioacoustics and the Earth Species Project. "Once our system can provide real-time marine mammal classifications, it could support a wide range of marine projects, including conservation, research, First Nations Guardian programs, and vessel strike prevention efforts," the team said. Project Sea Who's Calling will now advance to the global Grand Finale, taking place in Brest, France on December 10, 2026. Last year, the winning project from Canada's edition of Ocean Hackathon 9, also hosted by COAST and Ocean Networks Canada at COAST's Ocean Innovation Hub in Victoria, was the only one from North America to make it to the Grand Finale. Out of 57 teams worldwide, Ocean Drift took second place overall.

Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy Panama Canal Authority The Panama Canal reported growth in vessel traffic, tonnage and revenue in fiscal year 2026, as stronger demand from energy carriers and containerships helped lift volumes despite ongoing concerns over water availability. The waterway handled 13,951 vessel transits during the fiscal year ended September 30, up 4.1% from 13,404 the previous year, according to results released Wednesday by the Panama Canal Authority. Total tonnage climbed 6.5% to 521 million Panama Canal Universal Measurement System (PC/UMS) tons, compared with 489.2 million tons in fiscal 2025. Larger vessels continued to drive much of the growth. Ships using the canal’s Neopanamax locks accounted for 52.2% of total tonnage, with volumes through those locks increasing 8.2% year over year. The canal attributed the gains to stronger demand from energy shipping segments, solid containership performance and shifting international trade patterns. Financial results were even stronger, with total revenue reaching approximately $6.6 billion, up 16.6% from the previous year. The figures remain unaudited. The results come as the canal continues to balance growing shipping demand with water conservation measures designed to protect operations during the developing El Niño weather pattern. Despite the challenges, the canal maintained a maximum authorized draft of 50 feet throughout the fiscal year’s dry season, providing relatively stable operating conditions for shipping customers. “Far from restricting trade flows, the Panama Canal facilitates international maritime trade by providing its customers with a reliable and safe route,” Panama Canal Administrator Ilya Espino de Marotta said during a conference call hosted by Bank of America Merrill Lynch. The canal also announced Wednesday that it was immediately reinstating its Last-Minute Reservation service for vessels using the Panamax locks. The service allows vessels without existing reservations to secure a transit slot when one becomes available, although the canal retains discretion over whether to offer the additional capacity. The decision follows improvements in watershed conditions, with recent rainfall approaching average levels and water-saving measures helping conserve supplies. It marks another adjustment to operations following restrictions imposed earlier this year in response to below-normal rainfall. The canal recently increased daily booking capacity to 33 slots , including 10 Neopanamax slots, effective October 15. However, water availability remains a concern. The canal has warned that a continuing water deficit could require further operational adjustments, particularly if El Niño conditions intensify. During Wednesday’s call, canal executives also discussed longer-term infrastructure investments, including the proposed Río Indio Lake Project, a central component of the canal’s strategy to secure freshwater supplies for future operations. The project is part of the canal’s broader Vision 2025–2035 development plan, aimed at strengthening the waterway’s resilience and maintaining its competitiveness as global shipping patterns evolve. For now, the latest results show that the Panama Canal continues to attract growing volumes of shipping traffic, even as water management remains one of its biggest operational challenges. U.S. Army Photo By Chris Servello (OpEd) After years of testing and debating how unmanned surface vessels fit into the fleet, the Navy is starting to show what these systems can do. And there’s a lot to like. Recent operations in the Persian Gulf have demonstrated their value. The USS Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group has deployed with a medium unmanned surface vessel. Industry is delivering increasingly capable platforms. And senior leaders in the Department of War and Department of the Navy are talking less about the promise of unmanned warfare and more about making it part of everyday operations. That’s progress, and the Navy, its sailors and industry partners deserve credit. But now comes the harder part. The Navy needs to decide how it intends to fight with unmanned vessels, what missions they’ll perform and how it will organize, train and sustain the forces operating them. It’s time to move from proving these systems work to making them a routine part of fleet operations. Experimentation got us here. It remains important and should never stop. But experimentation alone isn’t a strategy, and continuing to treat it as one wastes time and money. The Right Signals From Leadership At this month’s Association of the United States Army conference, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth put autonomous warfare squarely on the department’s agenda. His Project Agincourt initiative and plans for an Autonomous Warfare Command are intended to accelerate how the military develops, buys and employs unmanned capabilities. Hegseth also emphasized something often overlooked in discussions about new technology: the need to change organizations, training and acquisition practices, not just buy equipment. The military has never lacked interesting technology. The challenge is turning it into something commanders can reliably use. Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao offered examples of where that transition is happening. At AUSA, Cao highlighted an unmanned surface vessel that helped recover two downed Army Apache aviators near the Strait of Hormuz. He also pointed to unmanned underwater systems supporting mine clearance and announced that the Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group had deployed with a medium unmanned surface vessel. These are meaningful developments. They show unmanned systems moving beyond demonstrations and into real missions. Cao described the technology as a force multiplier. That’s the right way to think about it. The goal isn’t simply more unmanned vessels in the water. It’s giving commanders more options, extending the fleet’s reach, reducing risk to sailors and freeing manned warships for missions that require them. The Persian Gulf Is Teaching Us Something Fifth Fleet deserves considerable credit for getting unmanned maritime operations to this point. For years, Task Force 59 worked with industry and regional partners to introduce unmanned systems into one of the world’s toughest maritime environments. Not every experiment succeeded, but the Navy learned how to operate these systems alongside manned forces, integrate their sensors and improve maritime awareness. That work is paying off. In June, when two Army aviators went down near Oman, a 24-foot Saronic Corsair unmanned surface vessel helped rescue them . The vessel recovered both soldiers and transported them to a location where they could be evacuated by helicopter. This wasn’t a demonstration. It was a real rescue, and two Americans came home because the Navy had the right capability in the right place. BlackSea Technologies, now part of AEVEX, offers another example. Its Global Autonomous Reconnaissance Craft, or GARC, extends surveillance and reconnaissance without requiring a manned warship for every mission. BlackSea also responded to an emerging operational requirement for unmanned mine countermeasure capabilities in the Persian Gulf. With mines threatening shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the Navy needed ways to address the danger without unnecessarily exposing sailors and expensive ships. BlackSea’s response illustrates the relationship the Navy needs with industry: identify an urgent problem, communicate the requirement and give companies an opportunity to deliver quickly. These examples matter for different reasons. Saronic showed what happens when an unmanned vessel is available for an unexpected emergency. BlackSea demonstrated how industry can respond to an emerging operational need. The Strait of Hormuz is an ideal place to learn. It’s crowded, geographically constrained and strategically important. Commercial shipping mixes with military operations, and threats can emerge quickly. It also reinforces a lesson worth remembering: unmanned vessels don’t have to be large, expensive or capable of doing everything. Sometimes a small platform performing one mission well is exactly what the fleet needs. But these lessons shouldn’t stay in the Persian Gulf. Fifth Fleet’s experience should help shape how the Navy employs unmanned vessels everywhere. Once a system demonstrates it can perform a useful mission, the next question should be how quickly we can get it to more commanders. Not how many more demonstrations we can schedule. The Theodore Roosevelt Deployment Matters The deployment of the Leidos-built Seahawk medium unmanned surface vessel with the Theodore Roosevelt strike group is another important step. Seahawk and its sister vessel, Sea Hunter, have spent years helping the Navy develop autonomous navigation, collision avoidance, communications and manned-unmanned operations. Now Seahawk is operating with a deployed carrier strike group. A carrier strike group isn’t a laboratory. It has missions, schedules and commanders who need equipment that works. An unmanned vessel must contribute without creating more problems than it solves. How does the commander employ it? Who controls it? What happens when communications are degraded? Who maintains it? How does it integrate with aircraft and surface combatants? What missions can it perform that free a destroyer, helicopter or aircraft for something else? Those questions matter. But they’re only the ones we know to ask today. One of the greatest benefits of this deployment may be discovering uses nobody anticipated. Put a new capability in the hands of experienced sailors and commanders, and they’ll find ways to employ it that engineers and requirements officers never considered. Maybe it’s an unexpected surveillance mission, a new way to extend the strike group’s reach or a task that would otherwise consume valuable flight hours or tie up a manned combatant. Some of the best ideas may emerge simply because Seahawk is available when an unexpected problem arises. The deployment will reveal problems, too. That’s fine. Better to find them during real operations than spend another five years trying to anticipate everything in a test environment. The Navy needs to capture both the expected and unexpected lessons and apply them quickly. Success shouldn’t simply mean Seahawk completes its deployment. It should mean the Navy comes away with a workable model for employing unmanned vessels across other formations, along with a better understanding of missions nobody originally envisioned. That’s how an experiment becomes a capability. And sometimes, how a new way of fighting begins. The Navy Needs a CONOPS It Can Man, Train and Equip To Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle has emphasized building a hybrid fleet that combines manned ships and unmanned systems. His fighting instructions identify scouting, screening and striking as important missions for medium unmanned surface vessels. That’s a good start. But the Navy needs to turn those broad missions into concepts of operations that commanders can execute and the service can organize around. Start with missions where the technology is reasonably mature: surveillance, scouting, screening, electronic warfare and selected logistics tasks. Continue developing more demanding missions, including strike and sea denial, as the technology and tactics improve. And resist the temptation to build one vessel that does everything. We’ve seen where that leads in traditional shipbuilding. Requirements grow, costs rise, schedules slip and the Navy waits years for a platform designed to solve every problem. Unmanned vessels offer a chance to do things differently. Establish common standards, define the missions and let industry compete to deliver solutions. Companies like Leidos, HII, Saronic and BlackSea bring different capabilities. That’s a strength, provided the Navy gives them clear requirements and a path to production. But the bigger challenge may be inside the Navy. Who owns these vessels? Who operates them? What training is required? How are crews certified? Who handles maintenance, spare parts and repairs? How does the Navy measure readiness? These questions aren’t as exciting as artificial intelligence or autonomous navigation, but they’re the difference between an operational capability and a science project. The Navy has started addressing some of this through dedicated unmanned organizations, personnel specialties and acquisition reforms. Now those efforts need to connect to actual force structure and deployment requirements. The service should be able to tell Congress how many vessels it needs, what missions they’ll perform, where they’ll be based, how they’ll deploy and what it costs to keep them operational. That’s what it means to man, train and equip a force. Keep Experimenting. Just Don’t Confuse It With a Strategy. None of this means slowing innovation. Technology is moving too quickly for the Navy to stop experimenting. Ukraine’s operations in the Black Sea have shown how relatively inexpensive unmanned systems can threaten much larger naval forces. The Middle East is producing its own lessons. Artificial intelligence, sensors, communications and autonomy will keep improving. The Navy must keep learning. But experimentation should improve an operational force, not substitute for one. We don’t stop deploying aircraft because better radars are being developed. We don’t keep destroyers in port while waiting for new missiles. We field what works, learn from operating it and make improvements. Unmanned vessels should be no different. Some systems will fail. Others won’t fit particular missions. Commanders will discover problems nobody anticipated. That’s part of developing capability. What’s harder to defend is spending another decade and billions of dollars experimenting without making the decisions needed to put these systems into routine service. At some point, experimentation without an operational plan becomes wasteful. And with the demands facing today’s Navy, wasted time may be more costly than wasted money. It’s Time to Make Some Decisions Secretary Hegseth, Acting Secretary Cao and Admiral Caudle have an opportunity to build on real momentum. The department is prioritizing autonomous warfare. The Navy is changing how it acquires unmanned systems. Fleet commanders are gaining experience, and industry is delivering capable platforms. Now the Navy needs a focused implementation plan. Within the next year, it should identify which missions are ready for routine operations, establish the organizations responsible for them and put the training, maintenance and sustainment systems in place to support deployment. Acquisition decisions should follow those operational requirements, not another round of disconnected demonstrations. Congress should support the effort while holding the Navy accountable for delivering usable capability. This doesn’t mean betting everything on today’s technology or choosing one company to build every vessel. It means making reasonable decisions with what we know and improving as we learn. The Navy has spent years working toward a hybrid fleet. Much of that work has been worthwhile, and recent developments suggest we’re closer than ever.

articles.title: Editorial: The Coast Guard Spent $3.8 Million on a PDF
articles.summary: The Coast Guard’s new credentialing portal promises complete applications and faster processing. One American ship captain tested it. What he found raises serious questions about automation, accountability, and whether Washington...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo of the USCG National Maritime Center The Coast Guard’s new credentialing portal promises complete applications and faster processing. One American ship captain tested it. What he found raises serious questions about automation, accountability, and whether Washington understands the problem it’s trying to solve. By an Anonymous U.S. Merchant Marine Captain Last April, President Trump signed Executive Order 14269, Restoring America’s Maritime Dominance . It’s a serious commitment to rebuilding the U.S. Merchant Marine, and tucked into Section 13 is an order every American mariner should care about: identify unnecessary or burdensome credentialing requirements and eliminate them. The White House understands something Washington has forgotten for decades. You can build all the ships you want, but without licensed mariners to sail them, they’re just expensive steel tied to a pier. Military Sealift Command has already had to scale back operations because it cannot find enough qualified crews. Anyone who has sailed aboard an MSC vessel understands what it means when a ship cannot get underway for lack of people. So when the Coast Guard launched NAVITA , its new merchant mariner credentialing portal, on September 14, there was good reason for optimism. As gCaptain reported in June , the Coast Guard tied the project directly to the executive order, and Rear Adm. Rob Compher said the goal was “to make it easier for mariners to get the credentials they need to work.” That’s exactly the right goal. For years, mariners have described the National Maritime Center in West Virginia as a bureaucratic black hole. This summer, more than 19,000 applications were reportedly sitting in the backlog, with processing times stretching eight to twelve months. I hold a Master Unlimited license. I spent over a decade at sea on tankers, containerships and MSC vessels, and I’ve been through the Coast Guard’s credentialing process myself. So I logged in and tested NAVITA. Here’s the short version. It doesn’t fix the problem. NAVITA does not appear to solve the problem it was designed to fix. The Coast Guard’s pitch is simple. NAVITA will speed things up by making sure every application is complete. It flags missing items as you go, it figures out your fees, and it connects to Pay.gov so you can pay on the spot. That sounds great on paper. The trouble is it’s solving a problem mariners don’t have, because the problem was never that we forget to include documents. It’s that the arcane and byzantine rules by which the Coast Guard governs credentials are so confusing to so many mariners that the information in the documents is often wrong. It’s paperwork that appears complete but contains information the Coast Guard will reject. And NAVITA, at least in its first release, appears unable to distinguish between the two. Talk to any mariner who’s been through a renewal and you’ll hear the same thing. Nobody forgets their physical. What trips people up is that the doctor has to initial and date every page, and a lot of doctors don’t know that, so the application comes back. Nobody forgets their drug test either. But plenty of mariners walk into a clinic and take whatever test the clinic offers, a 7, 9 or 12 panel, when the Coast Guard will only take the DOT 5-panel. Never mind that the other tests screen for more drugs, not less. Nobody forgets their sea service letters. What they don’t know to check is whether the tonnage on the letter matches what the National Vessel Documentation Center has on file, or whether the dates line up with the vessel’s records. Nobody tells you the evaluator is going to look. And nobody forgets to pay. NAVITA even has a fee widget to help with that. In my testing it gave me the wrong number, and more often than not it wanted me to pay more than I owed. So does NAVITA catch any of this? The answer is NO. It checks that a file is there. It doesn’t care what’s in it. That’s an important distinction when the entire purpose of the system is supposed to be reducing application errors. When I tested a renewal for a more complicated endorsement, NAVITA gave me a long list of “optional uploads.” Some had nothing to do with the application. Some were just wrong. Think about what that means for a mariner at home between hitches. The Coast Guard’s own website tells them they might need more training, so they sign up, pay for it and burn their time off doing it, for a requirement that doesn’t exist. Not really. NAVITA doesn’t check the data you type in. I entered an address that isn’t in the USPS database, and it took it without a word. That’s how your new credential ends up in somebody else’s mailbox. It doesn’t check your uploads either. It can’t tell if a scan is readable, if a page is missing or if you uploaded the wrong form. If the file ends in .pdf, it goes through. And if the tech team can’t get the if/then logic right on a fee calculator, how are they going to handle the much harder automation the Coast Guard keeps promising in the next release? I don’t have a clue. As gCaptain reported last September, the Coast Guard gave Stealth Solutions, a Salesforce consulting partner, a five-year deal worth up to $49.6 million to modernize credentialing . The first task order, $3.8 million, paid for the first release of NAVITA. Here’s what that first release does. It takes your information and turns it into a PDF. That’s it. There’s no back end. People familiar with the system tell me staff are re-entering the information from Salesforce into the NMC’s old system so evaluators can review it the same way they always have. So that’s $3.8 million for a PDF, with $45.8 million still left on the contract. The Coast Guard will tell you this is only the first release and the good stuff is coming. I’ve heard that one before. I shook my Magic 8 Ball on behalf of every mariner waiting in the queue, and it came up “Outlook not good.” And I have firends and family working for companies that use Saleforce. They tell me the company is famous for charging for additional unlocks. That might work for a large company raking in revenue but could cause an underfunded department like the NMC inside a budget anemic organization like the US Coast Guard to run into brick walls. From what I’ve been told, user testing was limited to a small group of service academy and union staff. A lot of them don’t work credentialing cases day to day, so they had no real way of knowing whether what NAVITA told them was right. Industry wasn’t brought in at all. The mariners and operators whose paychecks depend on this system didn’t see it until launch day. My two Navy friends looking to enter the industry after a career spent at sea on warships say they are thouroughly confused by the process. Uploads have to be PDFs. Not a photo, not a Word file. Just about every app on your phone can turn a picture into a PDF without you even noticing, but NAVITA can’t, because Salesforce doesn’t do that out of the box. Who owns a scanner in 2026? The Coast Guard will say paper is still an option. You can walk your application into a Regional Exam Center. There are 19 of them, 16 are open, and none of them are in the middle of the Pacific. And if you go looking for forms CG-719B and CG-719C on the NMC website, you’ll find the download links are gone. One friend who is caught in a doom loop was told he’ll need to submit a Freedom of Information Act request to get the contents of his file. So how exactly are mariners supposed to use the paper option? Credentialing is one of the most complicated things the Coast Guard does. Endorsements, sea time, medical standards and training rules all depend on one another. And the Coast Guard picked Salesforce, an expensive platform built to track sales leads, to run it. Anything Salesforce doesn’t do out of the box has to be custom built in Apex, Salesforce’s own programming language, which looks a lot like Java. Now the Coast Guard is locked in to one vendor, paying for every customization, and it still doesn’t have features you’d expect from any website in 2026, and they likely don’t have the budget to unlock the custom programing they need. There are also rumors circulating that Apex solutions is outsourcing work to Southeast Asia. Could the FBI background checks and the records of veterans be exposed to foriegn agents? Probably not but this is they type of question that could easily be addressed by USCG representatives visiting the gCaptain forum or providing regular updates via YouTube or social media to assuage concerns. A lot of companies handle credentials for their crews. They have to. If a mariner’s credential lapses, that person can’t work, and the ship may not sail. NAVITA only lets a mariner name an individual as a third party, even though the OMB-approved CG-719B form lets employers, unions and others do it. U.S.-flag operators crew the commercial fleet the Defense Department relies on for strategic sealift, so anything that hinders an employer from ensuring its crew is properly credentialed is a threat to strategic sealift. Employers can list jobs on the gCaptain job board but resumes have to be vetted and credentials checked before anyone is hired. NAVITA does not make that easy. And with so many US flagged ships doing critical national security jobs today, that’s a serious problem for our military. The executive order told the government to remove barriers for mariners. NAVITA adds new ones. Here’s my prediction. NAVITA will shorten the line in one way, and it’s not the way anyone intended. Experienced mariners who’ve renewed their papers for decades will take one look at this thing, give up and retire. A few years ago gCaptains founder Captain John Konrad wrote an editorial titled “ Admiral, I Am NOT Ready For War. ” His point then was that equipment doesn’t win wars, people do. That’s still true. We’re short of mariners right now, and every one we lose to a bad website is one fewer we’ll have when the country needs us. REUTERS/Nathan Howard The United States has imposed a new round of sanctions targeting a law firm, shipping agents and nine vessels accused of helping Iran move oil and other commodities through international markets, expanding Washington’s crackdown on the networks supporting Tehran’s shadow fleet. The U.S. Treasury Department announced the measures Wednesday as part of Operation Economic Outcast, an ongoing campaign aimed at cutting off Iran’s remaining sources of revenue amid the continuing conflict in the Middle East. At the center of the latest action is Karnakis and Karnakis, a law firm operating in Panama and Greece that Treasury says has spent years establishing shell companies used to conceal the ownership of vessels transporting Iranian petroleum, petrochemicals and steel. According to Treasury, the firm helped register shipping companies responsible for moving hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of Iranian commodities, including vessels connected to previously sanctioned entities. The law firm also played a key role in establishing the corporate network behind Iranian liquefied petroleum gas magnate Seyed Asadoollah Emamjomeh, whose shipping operations have transported hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of Iranian LPG and crude oil. Treasury sanctioned the firm and five associated individuals, accusing them of helping obscure the true ownership of companies involved in Iranian commodity shipments. The action represents a broader effort to target not just the vessels carrying sanctioned cargo, but also the legal, corporate and logistical services that allow shadow fleet operators to function. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that those supporting Iranian shipping operations would face consequences, saying, “if you are supporting the Iranian regime, we will find you and sanction you.” The latest designations also include Roxette Maritime Shipping and Trading S.A., a Panama- and Greece-based company for which Karnakis and Karnakis serves as corporate agent. Treasury identified Roxette as the operator and ship manager of seven Panama-flagged cargo vessels: ANEMOS, GLORIS, PRIDE, DESTINY, FLAMINGO 1, HARMONY and PRINCE. Three of those vessels — ANEMOS, GLORIS and PRIDE — carried Iranian-origin goods, including petrochemicals and steel products, within the past year, according to Treasury. All seven vessels were identified as blocked property under the new sanctions. The department also targeted two shipping agencies accused of facilitating Iranian cargo movements through international ports. Singapore-based Amigoz Singapore PTE. Ltd. allegedly provided port services for an Iranian light crude shipment connected to Sepehr Energy Jahan Nama Pars Company, which Treasury says helps channel billions of dollars’ worth of commodities to Iranian military entities. Amigoz was also linked to vessels associated with the shipping network of Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani and provided bunkering services to the previously sanctioned shadow fleet vessel ZIXUAN. Meanwhile, Dubai-based Whales Shipping Line LLC was sanctioned for its involvement with Amigoz. Treasury said Whales had also acted as a shipping agent for a sanctioned trading company involved in purchasing tens of millions of dollars’ worth of Iranian petrochemicals. Two UAE-flagged support vessels owned by Whales, WHALES DIAMOND and WHALES PEARL, were identified as blocked property. The measures are the latest under Operation Economic Outcast, launched on August 24 as part of the Trump administration’s campaign to isolate Iran economically. The effort has increasingly focused on the international network of ship managers, brokers, port agents, financial institutions and corporate service providers that support Iranian oil exports and sanctions evasion. Wednesday’s announcement also included a financial enforcement component. Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) said it was working with European partners, including authorities in Greece, to investigate a Greek bank’s potential connections to Iran and its proxies. The agency said it had issued its first administrative subpoena under a provision of the Bank Secrecy Act as part of that investigation, along with additional requests for information concerning banks’ relationships with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions. The latest sanctions come as Washington continues applying military and economic pressure on Iran, including efforts to restrict its maritime trade through the Strait of Hormuz. Join the leading maritime news network Stock Photo: Anita van den Broek Australia-based IFM Investors has agreed to acquire a controlling stake in Associated British Ports (ABP), the UK’s largest port operator, in a deal that values the company at approximately £10 billion ($13.4 billion). Under the agreement announced Wednesday , a fund managed by IFM Investors will purchase a combined 63.9% stake from two Canadian pension investors. Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPP Investments) will sell its 33.9% holding, while OMERS will exit its 30% stake. The companies did not disclose financial terms, although Bloomberg reported that the transaction values ABP at approximately £10 billion, citing a person familiar with the deal. ABP operates 19 port facilities across the UK, including major gateways at Southampton, Immingham and Hull. The company handles approximately 25% of the country’s seaborne trade and plays a significant role in supporting Britain’s energy sector, including more than half of its offshore wind capacity. The acquisition represents a major change in ownership for one of Britain’s most important maritime infrastructure businesses. OMERS has held its stake since 2006, while CPP Investments joined the ownership group in 2015. Kyle Mangini, global head of infrastructure at IFM Investors, said the investment would support continued development of ABP’s port infrastructure and operations. The deal also reflects growing interest among pension funds and infrastructure investors in port assets, which offer long-term exposure to international trade, energy infrastructure and industrial activity. IFM Investors, which is owned by Australian pension funds and the UK’s Nest pension scheme, manages approximately £157 billion in assets globally. The firm already has investments in port infrastructure around the world. ABP has continued investing in its facilities in recent years, including the Immingham Renewable Fuels Terminal, Green Port Hull and Southampton’s Horizon cruise terminal. Henrik L. Pedersen, chief executive of ABP, welcomed the agreement, describing the investment as an endorsement of the company’s business and long-term strategy. He said ABP intends to pursue further growth opportunities alongside IFM Investors and its remaining shareholders. CPP Investments and OMERS said the sale would allow them to realize the value of their long-term investments and redeploy capital into new opportunities. The transaction remains subject to customary shareholder and regulatory approvals, including national security review, and is expected to close in the first half of 2027. October 21, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Sunshine Seeds Urals crude prices at Russia's Baltic and Black Sea ports fell to their lowest levels in one and a half months this week, according to Reuters monitoring and LSEG data, as the dated Brent benchmark also weakened and freight costs stayed high. Free-on-board prices for Urals crude for loading at Primorsk, Ust-Luga and Novorossiysk this week fell to around $80 per barrel for the first time since early September. Increased supply in physical markets for prompt dates weakened the dated Brent benchmark. High freight costs also influenced Russian sellers' revenues, traders said. The availability of tankers and extreme war risks in the Black Sea and the Red Sea make shipping very expensive. Urals differentials also weakened in India, the main market for the grade, to near parity with dated Brent. Weak refining margins in Asia reduced buying appetite for crude. Fuel supplies to world's market have been restored in part by a US-Russia agreement for diesel supplies and China's increase of fuel exports. The Urals FOB prices jumped above $100 per barrel in September and October as a result of oil export disruption caused by the US-Israeli war with Iran. Urals crude at Russia's western ports jumped above $110 per barrel on September 16 to the highest level since April 2026. Changes in Urals prices have a significant impact on Russia's oil and gas tax revenues and overall budget income as they are an indicator used to calculate the oil extraction tax. REUTERS/Antranik Tavitian By Julian Lee (Bloomberg) — Oil shipments from the Middle East are showing little sign of buckling in the face of Iran’s more frequent and damaging attacks on merchant ships in the region. Crude and condensate flows from the Persian Gulf hit a high of 24.6 million barrels a day in the week to Oct. 18, according to data provider Kpler. However, shipments are volatile and figures for the average of October to date remain below prewar levels. Loadings tend to happen in bunches, with ships traveling in convoys through the Strait of Hormuz , shuttling cargoes to tankers waiting outside the waterway before returning to reload. Figures from rival data firm Vortexa don’t show the same weekly surge, highlighting the difficulty of establishing export levels as most tankers are currently operating with their positioning signals turned off. It pegs flows over the same seven-day period at 18 million barrels a day. Both companies estimate flows before the conflict was at least 18.5 million barrels a day. The continued strong volumes despite the Iranian attacks show the desire for Middle Eastern producers to keep moving their barrels. Oil forms the backbone of the countries’ economies and they’ve been competing for customers in recent months to make up for billions of dollars of missed sales during the conflict. For October so far, Kpler pegs Middle East flows at 16.7 million barrels a day, while Vortexa puts it at 15.4 million. Kpler aggregates its numbers from Hormuz transits, net flows via ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, exports through Red Sea ports and those on the Gulf of Oman in the United Arab Emirates and Oman. The Vortexa numbers sum shipments from Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Iran, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Oman. The resilience comes as producers including Iraq are sending more volumes through Hormuz while Saudi Arabia is sending oil out from both its Persian Gulf and Red Sea coast. The kingdom boosted production by a third in September to over 8 million barrels a day, recovering from the lowest in more than three decades in the previous month. The UAE, one of the most successful in moving tankers through Hormuz, has pushed its production to record-high levels, according to the International Energy Agency. These efforts appear to be holding up in spite of a spate of attacks in the waterway that’s also sunk at least one container ship this month. UK Maritime Trade Operations, a unit of the country’s navy, has reported 32 attacks on ships around the Arabian peninsula so far this month, compared with 16 in the whole of September. Some of these have struck ships’ engine rooms, inflicting more severe damage. “Attacks on merchant vessels around the Strait have increased sharply in recent weeks,” Morgan Stanley analysts including Martijn Rats wrote in a note. Still, “oil flow through the strait has remained relatively resilient,” they added. Shipments are proving strong with fleets owned by the producing countries and a few gutsy shipowners keeping crude flows close to last month’s levels that were the highest since the conflict began. The UAE, Saudi Arabia and Kuwait are among nations that have shuttled their oil through Hormuz in their own tankers, and delivered the cargo to customers’ vessels outside the strait. The levels are also significant because of the complete loss of Iran’s exports following a US blockade of the country’s ports. Both Kpler and Vortexa estimate the Islamic Republic was shipping close to 2 million barrels a day in February. The assessments of Mideast flows are subject to change as tankers operating in the Persian Gulf and Red Sea with their automatic information systems switched off make real-time tracking more complicated. The process is hampered further by the withholding of satellite imagery over the region. As a result, shipments are frequently only recorded several days after they occur, leading to upward revisions. The shuttling service and the tendency for tankers to move in convoys have also made exports lumpy at times, with brief surges followed by periods of relative slowdown. For example, satellite images of the biggest Saudi oil terminal in the Persian Gulf show five very large crude carriers loading at the seven moorings on Oct. 12 and 13, but the number had fallen to just one on Oct. 20. The pattern is similar at other oil ports in the Persian Gulf and on the Red Sea. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P.
